Based on David Rohl’s Book 'The Lords of Avaris'

(A New Chronology of the Pre-Christian Era of Western Civilization)

Today, the fact that the Indo-European peoples originated from tribes of the Armenian Highlands has already become widely recognized.

But historical scholarship is constantly moving deeper into the past, and many things are becoming more specific and refined. In this respect, D. Rohl’s book (David Rohl, The Gods of Avaris, Eksmo, 2011) is one of the most outstanding works of recent years.

It boldly challenged established stereotypes in Western scholarship, and what Armenian scholars had known for a long time is now being cautiously explored by Western historians as well. It has its own biases and obstacles, some of which we will discuss below. But the process is underway, and truth is ultimately indestructible, despite the spite of detractors and the mockery of the ignorant.

In this article, we present a brief overview of the book, highlighting those points that intersect with the ancient history of the Armenians. All statements quoted from the book are placed in quotation marks and accompanied by page references. Claims taken from other sources are specifically marked with references.

Let us begin our review of its main arguments.

“Tribes speaking Indo-European dialects first appeared on the historical stage in Eastern Anatolia” (p. 42).

Here, the origin of the Indo-European peoples is clearly stated. But why is Eastern Anatolia specified?

As E. Danielyan points out:

“According to the latest research in comparative linguistics, genetic linguistics, archaeology, anthropology, and historical geography, the Indo-European homeland included the Armenian Highlands (the cradle of the Armenian people), eastern Asia Minor, and northern Mesopotamia.

At the same time, it must be noted that the incorrect use of the terms ‘Eastern Anatolia’ and ‘South Caucasus’—instead of the western and eastern parts of the Armenian Highlands—distorts the toponymic terminology used in identifying and classifying linguistic and archaeological material.

In reality, the Caucasus, with all its parts—northern, southern, eastern, and western—and its foothills, lies to the north and east of the Armenian Highlands and the Kura River, while Anatolia, with all its parts—northern, southern, eastern, and western—is located within Asia Minor, to the west of the Armenian Highlands.”

From these scholarly positions, when approaching modern research based on archaeological and Indo-European linguistic data, one can state that materials presented under the terms “Anatolia” or “Anatolian” are falsified in Turkish and some foreign publications for political reasons. Instead of the western part of the Armenian Highlands, occupied by Turkey, the fabricated term “Eastern Anatolia” is used.

It is known that even the slightest reference to the name “Armenian Highlands” can result in a foreign archaeologist being denied permission by the Turkish authorities to participate in excavations conducted in Western Armenia.

D. Rohl is a prominent historian and archaeologist who personally conducted excavations in Egypt, the Middle East, and Turkey. In this book, he focuses on the history of the Hyksos and examines the period from 2000 to 800 BC, introducing a New Chronology of history that shifts the events described forward by 200–300 years, bringing them closer to the present.

Being a serious scholar and adhering strictly to scientific evidence, he was nevertheless repeatedly astonished by the fact that:

“Legendary histories that were repeatedly dismissed as fiction later proved to have a historical basis confirmed by archaeological discoveries” (p. 44).

Some of his conclusions contradict the conceptions of scholars such as T. V. Gamkrelidze and Vyach. Vs. Ivanov. According to their theory, the initial divergence of the Indo-European languages occurred no later than the 5th–4th millennia BC. This was the period when the Common Indo-European linguistic system existed, while its disintegration began at the end of the 4th millennium BC. In the 3rd millennium BC, the Greek-Armenian-Aryan dialect continuum emerged and subsequently split.

However, according to D. Rohl’s research, this linguistic unity still appears in the 8th century BC, continuing into the age of Homer and Hesiod, from which the separation supposedly begins.

D. Rohl’s main focus is not so much on the Hyksos themselves as on their significance for Western civilization.

Here is what he writes about them:

“The rule of the Hyksos in Egypt is a period closely connected with the roots of Western civilization… The Hyksos era is the historical basis for the Greek and Roman legends” (p. 47).

“After their departure from Egypt, the Hyksos became the forefathers of Hesiod’s Age of Heroes, celebrated in the ancient legends of Greece and Rome” (p. 88).

Where did the Hyksos come from? What language did they speak? What culture provided the rich heritage from which Western civilization drew?

“A group of Indo-European migrants arrived in Canaan in the Early Bronze Age. Graves and ornaments indicate an Anatolian origin. They came to power in the cities and became wealthy through maritime trade. Their descendants occupied Egypt under the name Hyksos” (p. 181).

But:

“The Hyksos did not speak the Egyptian language” (p. 134).

Thus, contrary to the version still prevalent today—that culture came to Greece and the Roman world from Egypt—we see D. Rohl pointing to entirely different origins for European civilization.

“The very first pharaohs came from Mesopotamia” (p. 199).

A particular type of burial was characteristic of this group: an elongated pit dug into the ground and lined with stone blocks. This type of tomb is distributed along a broad arc stretching from the Euphrates through Syria and Palestine to Transjordan and the Dead Sea. The Hyksos had the same type of burial (p. 181).

At the beginning of their migration from the Armenian Highlands, the Hyksos settled in the lands of Palestine and, as D. Rohl points out:

“Rephaim and Anakim—Hurrian names and tribes—appear in the Levant in 2100 BC” (p. 179).

“They were skilled in metalworking” (p. 180).

In other words, they brought with them a culture of metalworking.

The Hyksos were closely connected with the Phoenicians (p. 128), if one does not go so far as to suggest that they themselves were the famous Phoenicians.

“Remnants of the Hyksos retained their presence in Palestine” (p. 150)

even later.

“A large group of Hurrian Hyksos who settled in Jerusalem were the biblical Jebusites” (p. 153)—the Essenes.

For example:

“The Jebusite ruler Aruvana of Jerusalem” (p. 153).

We know that it was among the Essenes that ideas resembling Christianity first emerged, or were inherited by them from their ancestors.

But migrants from the Highlands did not settle only in Palestine. They also inhabited a number of islands in the Mediterranean.

“Clans of Indo-European seafarers inhabited Cyprus and Crete; later they moved to Egypt and ruled there under the name Hyksos, and after their expulsion they appeared in Palestine under the name Peleset—the Philistines, the Sea Peoples” (p. 187).

“The king of the Philistines—Abimelech” (p. 183).

Thus, they returned once again and remained in Palestine, fearing the growing power of Assyria, which they would have had to cross in order to return to their ancestral Highlands.

“After leaving Egypt, these shemau of the Philistia of the Late Bronze Age became the seranim—the rulers of the five cities—Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron” (p. 192).

“The inhabitants of Jerusalem—the Solomites according to Manetho, that is, the Solymi—from Anatolia. They are from the Anakim and Rephaim” (p. 370).

Many authors testify to the departure of the Hyksos from Egypt. However, D. Rohl believes that there was no actual expulsion.

“There was no mass exodus from Egypt. These were the same people who had lived there previously” (p. 69).

At the same time, it is known that:

“The great Hyksos dynasty—the 15th Dynasty—was expelled from Egypt by Pharaoh Ahmose, founder of the 18th Dynasty, in 1181” (p. 47).

Is there a contradiction between these facts?

D. Rohl insists that this was merely an ordinary dynastic division, of the kind that repeatedly occurred in Hyksos history.

“Queen Ahhotep, mother of Ahmose, the victor over the Hyksos, was a Pelasgian princess. The Greek legend of Io and Telegonus raises the intriguing possibility that Ahhotep was also the mother of the Hyksos king Apophis.

In that case, Ahmose and Apophis were half-brothers, fighting for control of the Nile Delta in what was essentially an intra-dynastic struggle between the country’s ruling elites” (p. 216).

Stories of intra-dynastic struggles for power are extremely common in ancient history. One need only recall the history of the Parthian Empire or the Byzantine Empire to discover the typical features shared by such family divisions.

The other pharaohs were also related to the Hyksos.

“The dynasty of Ramesses II originated from Avaris” (p. 125).

“Ramesses I had Hyksos ancestry” (p. 125).

Even:

“The god Set was also from Avaris.”

“Seti I, father of Ramesses II, celebrated the 400th anniversary of Set’s coronation as ruler of Avaris” (p. 126).

“Ramesses II ascended the throne in 943 BC. The first year of Tutankhamun’s reign was 1007” (p. 126).

And:

“The foundation of the Temple of Set in Avaris [was] in 1385” (p. 127).

Later, in a similar manner, Armaeus-Danaus, who founded the tribe of the Danaans and the city of Adana, was expelled by his brother Egyptus.

If it is true that Egyptus had fifty sons, as Aeschylus says in his tragedy The Suppliants, where he describes the return of the daughters of Danaus to Argos, then Egyptus certainly did not need a rival brother when he had to divide power among fifty sons.

A stone vase bearing the cartouche of Apophis was discovered in a Phoenician burial site in Spain.

“Probably this vessel was a family relic belonging to a family connected by kinship with the Hyksos, who migrated in the 8th century BC during the colonizing movement from east to west” (p. 217).

Probably, this is how the Basques came into being—a people whose language preserved a connection with the toponyms of the Armenian Highlands.

The similarity between Hyksos culture and a number of famous civilizations preserved in human memory—such as the Atlantic, Minoan, Spartan, and ancient Greek civilizations—is confirmed by the facts cited by D. Rohl.

“Minoan frescoes were discovered in the palace of the Hyksos. Labyrinth-like patterns and images of bulls and bull-leaping were also discovered there” (p. 230).

But it is known that the earliest labyrinth-like form was found in the Armenian Highlands and represents a repeated image of the swastika.

“The frescoes from Avaris depict bull-leaping and struggles between humans and bulls. All of this appears against a labyrinth-like background” (p. 196).

“The word labyrinth derives from the Minoan labrys, meaning a double-headed axe used in sacred rituals in the Aegean” (p. 197).

There were no such bull fights in Egypt.

“Bull-leaping—the entertainment of the local nobility” (p. 339).

“This tradition originated in Anatolia” (p. 339).

Minoan civilization had a tragic ending. D. Rohl describes it as follows:

“Not far from the island of Crete lies the island of Thera. On this island is the settlement of Akrotiri, which faces toward Crete. It was destroyed by an earthquake followed by a volcanic eruption” (p. 257).

“1210–1181 BC—Akrotiri was destroyed by a volcanic eruption. In 1020–1100 BC, the city was abandoned. Mycenaean Greeks overthrew the native Minoan rulers of central Crete” (p. 259).

“The military power of the Minoan thalassocracy was destroyed by the eruption. The palaces and cities were protected by the fleet and had no fortification walls.

Ten years later, the Mycenaeans prepared ships and invaded and devastated the remnants of the Minoan cities” (p. 262).

“The Minoans belonged to the Atlantic culture, which oppressed the Athenians and fought against them” (p. 260).

“Thus, memories of the disappearance of Minoan civilization survived in the legend of Atlantis” (p. 262).

But what connection existed between the Minoans and the migrants from the Armenian Highlands? Who were the Mycenaean “Greeks,” and were they actually Greeks at all? And can the Atlantic civilization be connected with Armenia?

D. Rohl’s account of the history of the island of Akrotiri points to the possibility of such a connection.

“A Hurrian king ruled on the island of Akrotiri” (p. 270).

“A fresco from Akrotiri depicts a fleet traveling from the island of Thera to the Levant, concluding a peace treaty with a local Aryan or Hurrian ruler, and then the warriors—the shemau—staying in Avaris among the Hyksos. Afterwards, they return to their homeland on the islands of the Aegean Sea” (p. 277).

“They receive a warm welcome from their kinsmen on Calliste in Akrotiri approximately 80 years before the final eruption” (p. 278).

And here is the key fact that we will examine in detail:

“The leader’s palanquin is decorated with symbols indicating the title h/k—‘ruler of the mountain lands,’ which was borne by the Hyksos who ruled Egypt” (p. 279).

It was precisely from this combination of the two letters that the term Hyksos originated.

As D. Rohl says in connection with another case:

“For the first time in the history of Egyptian archaeology, a monumental hieroglyphic text included the title h/k—Kasout (literally ‘ruler of the mountain lands,’ but usually translated as ‘ruler of foreign lands’)—from which Manetho’s term Hyksos derives” (p. 233).

We know Manetho’s writings through the adaptations of Josephus Flavius. Let us examine in greater detail the history of the interpretation of these two letters.

First of all, it should be noted that one of the explanations given by Josephus himself is that the ending -sos belongs to the Greek language in which Josephus wrote and indicates the plural form.

In the singular, names receive the ending -os.

This is how Josephus himself explains it:

“In the Scriptures all names have been adapted for the convenience of the readers to the Greek manner, so that they would be easier [to pronounce]. But to us this type of naming seems inappropriate, and therefore among us both the forms and the endings of words remain unchanged: for example, Noah (Noeos) is called [among us] Noe, and this form is used throughout our writings.”

In another version of Manetho’s history, Josephus finds yet another explanation for the name Hyksos:

“In another copy I found that the sound ‘I’ (ai—E.G.) ‘ik’ signifies not kings, but, on the contrary, indicates that the shepherds were captives, since on the other hand Hik and Hak [pronounced with a strong aspiration] in Egyptian directly mean ‘captives.’”

“This explanation seems to me more plausible and more consistent with ancient history.”

The mention of the sound “I” (ai) appears only in Josephus’s book published in 1895 and reprinted by a mimeograph process in 2000.

Attempting to verify the accuracy of the transmitted pronunciation, we discovered that in Internet versions, and even in the recently published substantial anthology History of the Ancient East, edited by V. I. Kuzishchin (HIE, Moscow, 2002), approved as a textbook for historians, the sound “ai” does not appear.

Was this done intentionally, or was it simply the result of publishers’ inattention?

Knowing how prejudiced Russian publishers are toward mentioning anything Armenian, and how even in Byzantine history—thoroughly permeated by Armenian influence—they often strive not to mention Armenians, we accepted this “omission” as yet another, one of countless distortions. Let the publishers and editors of St. Petersburg University be ashamed of it—we decided to search for the truth in other editions.

Only after turning to the ancient Greek text of Josephus, a copy of the original published in Germany in 1955—Flavii Iosephi, Opera V, Apud Weidmannos, vol. V, Contra Apionem Libri, Berlin, Germany, 1955, pp. 14–15—did we confirm the accuracy of the pre-Soviet translation, which had not yet been affected by “hard-line” chauvinism.

The diacritical marks above the letters in Ancient Greek indicated the diphthong ai. They are not used in the modern Greek language.

Incidentally, such distortions are characteristic not only of Soviet scholarship but of Western scholarship as a whole when it concerns Armenian history.

For example, D. Rohl states:

“Egyptologists always insert the letter e wherever there may be a vowel in a word. It has become customary to vocalize vowel symbols such as omega—w—as the letter u. For example, ‘house’ is pronounced by Egyptologists as ‘hut,’ although in many cases this letter is pronounced as ‘a.’ For example, Avaris sounds like Havare” (p. 500).

According to Josephus, Avaris, “according to an ancient religious tradition, was called” Hut-Uart, that is, “the house of the Uarts.”

But if, instead of the letter u, we substitute a, as Rohl corrects it, then there is no Urartu at all. There is Ararat, and the exact name of Avaris becomes “the house of the Ararats.”

Let us now attempt to determine what the Hyksos actually called themselves.

Let us return to their self-designation, “Hik” or “Hak,” which, according to Manetho and Josephus, was pronounced with aspiration and most likely should have sounded like “Hik” or “Hak.”

SIGN IN
[] First launch opens a browser for authentication
[] Headless or remote: grok login --device-auth
[] Or: export XAI_API_KEY="xai-..." then grok
[] Sign out: grok logout
[] In TUI: /login and /logout

START A SESSION
[] cd your-project then grok
[] First prompts: Explain this repo. or src/main.rs Walk me through this file.
[] grok -p "Explain this codebase" for a one-shot headless run
[] grok -c continues the most recent session in this directory
[] grok -r resumes a session by id (or the most recent)
[] grok inspect shows discovered config, skills, plugins, hooks, and MCP
[] grok models lists available models
[] Switch model in TUI with /model

LEARN THE TOOL
[] Run /tutorial or /help
[] /release-notes or /changelog for the current version
[] Read AGENTS.md in the repo (also CLAUDE.md if you are migrating)
[] Import Claude settings with /import-claude
[] Carry over rules, skills, and MCP from Claude / Cursor / Codex
[] Keyboard shortcuts: /help and Ctrl+.
[] Voice: Ctrl+Space or /voice
[] Shift+Tab cycles Plan, Auto, Always-approve

HOW TO WRITE A TASK
[] Outcome: what should be finished
[] Sources: files, folders, URLs, or mentions
[] Constraints: what not to touch, and when to ask
[] Deliverable: diff, report, test, or published app
[] Review point: plan first, or stop before commit/push
[] For big work: /plan first, then approve
[] For long ownership: /goal
[] For research first: /deep-research
[] For a sick laptop: tell it what is broken and let it investigate
[] Testers (tetsuo): start with work you can check — name the behavior, give a reproduction command, limit files, list final checks, say where to stop
[] Testers (tetsuo): inspect first (git status --short, grok inspect); give executable feedback (compiler/linter/tests) so the agent can loop; review the full diff and the command behind every green check

CORE COMMANDS
[] /new starts a new session
[] /home returns to the welcome screen
[] /resume and /sessions switch sessions
[] /fork branches the current session
[] /rename or /title names the session
[] /session-info shows session details (click or drag to copy)
[] /context shows token and skill/MCP cost
[] /usage shows credits
[] /compact condenses history
[] /rewind truncates conversation history (confirms; does not wipe files)
[] /export saves the conversation
[] /btw asks a side question without derailing the turn (v1.0.28: also works mid-message — text after `/btw` is the side question and stays out of the main transcript)
[] /check-work has a subagent review the code
[] /feedback files a report
[] /doctor and grok doctor fix terminal, tmux, clipboard, keyboard
[] grok du shows disk use under ~/.grok
[] grok wrap runs a command with local clipboard support
[] grok trace exports debug traces
[] /loop runs a prompt on an interval (auto-expires after 7 days)
[] Queued follow-ups can send as interjections if you turn that setting on
[] Ctrl+4 opens the Agent Dashboard
[] Ctrl+U can continue a Claude Code session inside Grok Build

PLAN MODE AND PERMISSIONS
[] /plan or Shift+Tab enters plan mode
[] Only the plan file can be edited until you approve
[] Auto and always-approve do not skip plan review
[] a approves, s requests changes, c comments, q quits plan
[] /view-plan reopens the preview
[] /auto auto-approves safer tools
[] /always-approve skips most prompts (deny rules and hooks still apply)
[] Edit always-allow bash as free-form globs
[] Restrict web search domains with [toolset.web_search] in config.toml
[] PreToolUse hooks can rewrite tool input, not only allow or deny
[] StopCancelled reports when a turn is interrupted or rejected
[] Pin auth to API key or OIDC in config.toml if needed

PARALLEL WORK AND AGENTS
[] Agent Dashboard: /dashboard or Ctrl+4
[] Run feature, review, fix, and test agents from one place
[] Pause, check progress, and jump into any agent
[] Worktrees: grok -w or Ctrl+W (isolated git copy under ~/.grok/worktrees)
[] grok worktree list / show / rm / gc
[] /fork --worktree forks into a worktree
[] /goal owns a long engineering objective (status, pause, resume, clear)
[] /create-workflow authors a repeatable multi-agent pipeline
[] /workflow launches, pauses, resumes, or stops a run
[] /workflows is the live run dashboard
[] /deep-research starts a built-in research workflow
[] Tools and MCP servers receive GROK_SESSION_ID
[] Background tasks and TODOs survive compaction

VOICE AND MEDIA
[] Dictate with Ctrl+Space
[] /imagine generates an image
[] /imagine-video generates a video
[] Ask it to boost, compress, and re-encode video audio in plain English
[] One-prompt 3D: ask it to model in Blender and watch it drive the app
[] Morning voice-memo automations can research and read you a briefing
[] Disable image/video tools via config or env if you do not want them
[] Testers: save preferred image/video edit designs and workflows as skills so repeats match your style

SKILLS PLUGINS AND MCP
[] /marketplace installs plugins
[] /plugins /skills /hooks /mcps open the same extensions modal
[] Skills live in ./.grok/skills, ~/.grok/skills, and plugin skill folders
[] User skills appear as slash commands; use /local:name if names collide
[] grok plugin install / enable / disable
[] grok mcp list / add / doctor
[] Type / to reference a skill
[] Testers: save preferred designs and editing workflows as skills so Grok Build reuses your style every time
[] Common marketplace plugins: Exa, TinyFish, MongoDB, Vercel, Sentry, Cloudflare, Chrome DevTools, Supabase, Neon, Firecrawl, Figma, Railway, Stripe

How AI Is Redefining Fashion Trend Agencies

AI is changing fashion trend agencies from trend reporters into trend interpreters.

Instead of relying only on seasonal research, agencies can now analyse huge volumes of runway imagery, social conversations, consumer behaviour and market signals to discover emerging patterns faster. The real value, however, is no longer simply finding what is popular—it is understanding which signals actually matter. (FashionUnited)

AI can identify a rising colour, silhouette or aesthetic, but fashion still needs human judgement to understand its cultural meaning, emotional relevance and commercial potential. This is particularly important as AI can push different agencies toward similar conclusions when they work from similar datasets. (FashionUnited)

The next generation of trend agencies will therefore combine data intelligence with human taste. Their role will shift from producing static trend reports to creating continuously updated, brand-specific insights and creative directions.

India is already moving in this direction. NIFT’s VisioNxt combines AI with Emotional Intelligence and on-ground trendspotting to create India-specific fashion forecasts. (https://t.co/6tEtYyjWhF)

The future isn’t about AI replacing the trend forecaster.

It’s about giving the forecaster a stronger lens and allowing human creativity to decide what the data cannot see.

AI can find the signal.
Fashion experts give it meaning.
Creativity turns it into the next movement.

Uno shows a simple way to speed up existing LLMs without changing their output distribution: keep the original model in charge, and use diffusion only to draft multiple tokens in parallel.

Keep the autoregressive model for quality and add diffusion for parallel drafting

On Qwen3-8B, Uno delivered 2.5X higher per-request throughput and 1.6X higher system throughput at the largest tested batch size.

Normal autoregressive LLMs generate 1 token at a time, making long responses, agents, and RL rollouts slow.

Uno adds lightweight diffusion adapters that propose several future tokens at once, while the original model verifies them.

That avoids a separate draft model and preserves the base model’s sampling behavior.

It also sped up end-to-end RL training by up to 40% in the reported runs.
